nameStory: The common name for Cribrinopsis similis isn't well established, as this species is often simply called the 'northern red anemone' or 'similar anemone.' The scientific name tells the real story - 'Cribrinopsis' means 'sieve-like appearance,' referring to the tiny pores that dot its column, while 'similis' means 'similar,' indicating how much this species resembles its relatives.
description: This is a chunky, colorful sea anemone that looks like an underwater flower when its tentacles are extended. The body (called a column) is typically brick-red to orange-red with a crown of thick, stubby tentacles surrounding the mouth. It can grow quite large for a New England anemone, reaching up to 4 inches across the tentacle crown and standing about 3 inches tall. When disturbed, it quickly pulls in its tentacles and becomes a smooth, dome-shaped blob stuck to the rocks.

idTips.label: Column texture
idTips.description: The body feels firm and rubbery to gentle touch, with tiny visible pores scattered across the red or orange surface that give it a slightly pitted texture like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Tentacle shape
idTips.description: Tentacles are thick, blunt, and relatively short compared to other anemones, feeling substantial and meaty rather than delicate when accidentally brushed

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Rich brick-red to orange-red coloration throughout, sometimes with darker red stripes running vertically down the column

idTips.label: Size and bulk
idTips.description: Noticeably chunky and substantial-looking, much more robust and thick-bodied than the common green anemones found in tide pools

idTips.label: Attachment strength
idTips.description: Grips rocks extremely firmly with its base - attempting to move one feels like trying to peel off a strong suction cup

habitat: Found in deeper tide pools and subtidal rocky areas along New England's coast, typically 10-60 feet underwater. Prefers areas with strong water movement and attaches to solid rock surfaces, often in crevices or under overhangs where it's protected from direct wave action. Most commonly encountered by divers or in very deep tide pools during extreme low tides.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters begin to warm, with tentacles fully extended for feeding. This is when they're easiest to spot and photograph with full tentacle display.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with maximum tentacle extension and vibrant coloration. Best time for observation during extreme low tides.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may begin retracting more frequently as water temperatures drop. Colors remain vibrant through early fall.
seasonality.winter: Often contracted into dome shape for extended periods, making identification more challenging. Still present but less conspicuous.

funFact: This anemone can live for over 60 years in the same exact spot on a rock, and if you were to return to the same tide pool decades later, you might find the great-great-grandchildren of the fish it's catching today swimming around as its potential future meals.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the northern red anemone (Urticina crassicornis), but Cribrinopsis similis has the distinctive tiny pores scattered across its column that look like pin-pricks, while Urticina has a smoother column surface. Memory trick: 'Cribrinopsis has a crispy, pitted surface.'
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Cribrinopsis is often mispronounced - it's 'CRIB-rin-OP-sis' with emphasis on the third syllable. Despite being called sea anemones, these animals are more closely related to corals and jellyfish than to the flower anemones they're named after.
compareHints: Since this is the only Cribrinopsis species commonly found in New England waters, compare it to other large anemones in the family. Unlike the smooth-columned Urticina species, Cribrinopsis similis has that distinctive perforated appearance with visible pores across its surface. It's also generally more orange-toned than the deeper red Urticina crassicornis, and tends to be found in slightly deeper water.
